title: Olympic Sports
description: Ten informative texts and profiles about the Olympic world: the ancient Games, the modern revival, the physics of skating jumps and the pole vault, rowing, curling, the marathon, the profile of an archer, the Paralympic movement and a museum's Olympic room.

lessons.title: The Games at Olympia
lessons.summary: How the ancient Games at Olympia worked, who ran them and what visitors endured.
lessons.text:
Every four years, for more than a thousand years, people from all over the Greek world made the long journey to Olympia, a sanctuary of the god Zeus in the green hills of southern Greece. The first Games that the Greeks recorded took place there in 776 BC, and most histories of the Olympics still begin with that date.

The Greeks, however, liked older stories. In their mythology, the Games were far more ancient than any record. One myth said that the hero Heracles had founded them and measured the stadium with his own feet. Another told of a young man named Pelops, who won a chariot race against a cruel king. Mythology gave the festival a grand past.

For a long time there was only one event, a footrace of about 192 meters, the length of the stadium. Later came longer races, wrestling, boxing and races for horses. In the stadium at Olympia, which visitors can still walk across, the old starting line remains: a row of long stone slabs with two grooves cut into them, where runners placed their toes.

It was the job of judges from the city of Elis, which controlled Olympia, to supervise the Games. To supervise thousands of proud competitors was not easy, and they could punish cheats with a whip or a heavy fine. The fines paid for bronze statues of Zeus, which stood in a row near the entrance to the stadium, each carrying the name of the cheat who had paid for it.

Olympia was also a place of rich buildings. The great Temple of Zeus, according to an ancient guidebook, was built with booty that Elis had taken from a neighbor in war. Other cities brought booty there too, and they liked to dedicate shields and statues to the god. Winners were allowed to dedicate statues of themselves, and these showed muscular young bodies in bronze and marble. Such muscular figures, copied many times, still shape how we picture an athlete.

The prize was simple: a crown of leaves from a sacred olive tree. The fame, though, was enormous, and not everyone approved. Lucian, a writer of satire, described a foreign visitor who watches young Greeks wrestling in the mud and cannot see the point. Satire of this kind shows that the Games had critics as well as fans.

Watching was hard work. The festival took place in high summer, crowds slept in tents, and there were few wells. Heat and thirst were part of the experience until, in the second century AD, a rich man built a fountain that finally brought fresh water to the site and ended the worst of the thirst.

Most of what we know comes from a small corpus of texts: poems written for winners, the guidebook of a traveler named Pausanias and lists of winners. Every season of digging adds to that corpus.

Questions:
When did the first recorded Games take place?
The first recorded Games took place at Olympia in 776 BC.
What can visitors still see at the starting line?
They can see long stone slabs with two grooves where runners placed their toes.
Whose job was it to supervise the Games?
It was the job of judges from Elis to supervise the Games.
How was the Temple of Zeus paid for?
It was built with booty that Elis had taken from a neighbor in war.
Why did visitors suffer from thirst?
The festival took place in high summer, and there were few wells.

lessons.title: A Frenchman's Dream
lessons.summary: How Pierre de Coubertin revived the Games, and the contradiction at the heart of his dream.
lessons.text:
Pierre de Coubertin was born in Paris in 1863 into a noble family. France had been badly defeated in a war in 1871, and Coubertin believed that French schools trained the mind but neglected the body. On visits to England he watched boys at schools such as Rugby play team games for hours, and he came home convinced that sport could build character.

Soon he began to envision something much larger than school sports. He had read about the ancient Games at Olympia, and he envisioned a modern festival, held every four years in a different city, where young people from many nations would meet in peaceful competition. Sport, he hoped, would create goodwill between countries that had too often met only on the battlefield.

In 1894 he gathered delegates at the Sorbonne in Paris, and they agreed to found the International Olympic Committee. The inaugural Games were held in Athens in April 1896. About 240 athletes from 14 nations took part, and the ancient marble stadium of Athens, restored with money from a rich Greek merchant, was filled with vibrant crowds. The marathon, a new race, became the heart of the inaugural Games when a Greek runner won it.

Every athlete at those first Games was a man, and that was exactly what Coubertin wanted. Like many people of his time and class, he saw sport as a manly activity that prepared boys to become strong citizens and soldiers. He wrote that events for women would be improper and dull to watch. Today it is hard to miss the contradiction: a man who dreamed of bringing the whole world together shut out half of it.

The next two Games did not go as he had envisioned. In Paris in 1900 and in St. Louis in 1904, the Olympics were attached to world's fairs and stretched over months, and some competitors did not even know that they were at the Olympics. Coubertin would later lament that his idea had almost disappeared among the exhibits of the fairs. Alas, his lament was justified: for a few years it seemed that the Games might not survive.

They did survive, and they slowly changed. Women first competed in 1900, in sports such as tennis and golf, but their progress was gradual, one event at a time over more than a century. The gradual change reached a milestone in Paris in 2024, when, for the first time, equal numbers of places were given to men and to women. Alas, Coubertin, who died in 1937, did not live to see how old-fashioned his manly ideal would come to look, or how much goodwill the women's events would earn.

At his own request, his heart was buried in a monument at Olympia, close to the ruins that had inspired him. Each time the Olympic flame is lit there for its journey to a vibrant host city, the first runner carries it to the monument that holds the heart of the man who brought the Games back.

Questions:
What did Coubertin envision?
He envisioned a modern festival, held every four years in a different city, where young people from many nations would meet.
Where and when were the inaugural modern Games held?
They were held in Athens in April 1896.
What was the contradiction in Coubertin's dream?
He dreamed of bringing the whole world together, but he shut women out of the Games.
Why did Coubertin lament the Games of 1900 and 1904?
They were attached to world's fairs, and his idea almost disappeared among the exhibits.

lessons.title: Four Turns in the Air
lessons.summary: A young skater's jumps explain torque, spin and the force of landing.
lessons.text:
From the stands, a figure skating jump looks like magic. A skater races backward, rises, spins into a tight blur and lands on one thin blade. In fact, every jump is a small lesson in physics, and Hannah Brooks, 17, who trains near Denver, can explain it better than most teachers.

There are six main jumps, and they differ mostly in the takeoff. Some start from the edge of the blade; others use the toe pick, the small teeth at the front of the blade. The axel is the only jump that starts while the skater is moving forward, so it needs an extra half turn.

Everything begins with torque, the twisting force that starts a body turning. As Hannah takes off, her blade pushes against the ice while her arms and free leg swing around her body. Together they produce the torque that sets her spinning. Once she leaves the ice, though, nothing can add more torque, so the amount of spin she carries is fixed until she lands.

How, then, does she turn faster in the air? Strangely, she does it by making herself smaller. When she pulls her arms tight against her chest and crosses her legs, her body's mass moves closer to the center of the spin, and she turns faster, just as someone on an office chair spins faster after pulling in their arms. In a good quad jump a skater makes more than five turns a second, which is astonishing for a human body. To slow down before landing, Hannah does the opposite: she begins to widen her arms and open her legs, and the spin eases. If she starts to widen too early, she falls short; if she waits too long, she crashes.

The landing is where her physiology is really tested. She comes down on one blade with a force of several times her body weight. Her knee and hip bend deeply, and the absorption of that force by her muscles protects her bones. Poor absorption, repeated thousands of times, leaves skaters susceptible to injuries in the ankles, knees and back, and young skaters whose bones are still growing are especially susceptible. Coaches who understand physiology therefore limit the number of jumps that a teenager practices each day. A speedy return after an injury is risky.

Hannah still remembers her first triple. It was frightening: the world turned too fast to see, and she was down before she knew where the ice was. Strangely, the frightening feeling disappeared within a few weeks. What remains now is timing, a speedy rotation and a soft landing.

For years, skaters spoke of the quad axel, four and a half turns, as a kind of unicorn: everyone discussed it, but no one had ever landed one in competition. In 2022 a teenager from the United States finally did it, an astonishing moment for the sport. Hannah is not chasing that unicorn yet. She has a triple axel to master first.

Questions:
What is torque, and where does Hannah's torque come from?
Torque is the twisting force that starts a body turning; it comes from her blade and her swinging arms and leg.
How does Hannah turn faster in the air?
She pulls her arms tight against her chest and crosses her legs.
What does she do to slow down before landing?
She begins to widen her arms and open her legs.
Why are young skaters especially susceptible to injuries?
Their bones are still growing.

lessons.title: Bending Toward the Sky
lessons.summary: The physics of the pole vault and how better poles changed the event.
lessons.text:
The pole vault looks like a trick. An athlete runs with a long pole and is suddenly flying over a bar as high as a rooftop. In fact, the event is one of the clearest examples of energy changing its form, and its physics is simple.

It starts with the run. A top athlete reaches a speed of around 10 meters a second. That speed is energy of motion. As the takeoff becomes imminent, the athlete lowers the tip of the pole into a small metal box set into the track. The pole then bends, sometimes into almost a half circle, and stores much of the energy of the run, the way a bow stores energy when its string is drawn. As the pole straightens, it gives that energy back and lifts the athlete upward. The athlete swings the legs up, turns upside down and rises along the pole like a kite climbing on a strong wind. At the top, for a moment, the body hangs almost still, like a kite on a calm afternoon, before a final push sends it over the bar.

Because the energy comes from the run, height shows a strong dependence on speed. A person running at 10 meters a second carries enough energy to lift the body about 5 meters. Add the height of the body's center at takeoff and the final push, and you reach about 6 meters, roughly the height of the rooftop of a two-story house and close to where the best men in the world now jump. Statistically, the fastest runners in the event tend to clear the highest bars, so coaches watch speed closely; statistically, it is one of the best signs of how high an athlete can go.

The dependence on equipment is just as strong. Early athletes used heavy wooden poles. Around 1900, they switched to bamboo, which was lighter and bent a little, and for decades bamboo was the standard. The best vault ever made on bamboo, in 1942, was about 4.77 meters. During the Second World War, the supply of good bamboo from Asia was cut off, and metal poles took its place.

Then, around 1960, came the advent of fiberglass poles. They bent far more than bamboo or metal and returned the energy smoothly. After their advent, records began to rise again, and by 1970 the best athletes were clearing about 5.5 meters.

Greater heights brought new dangers. For many years athletes landed in pits of sand or sawdust, which were unsafe once the bars rose above four meters. Thick foam mats soon became standard. Even today, officials check that the mats are wide enough, because landing beside them is unsafe. When an athlete feels that a failed jump is imminent, athletes are taught to push the pole away so that it does not fall on top of them.

Questions:
What happens to the energy of the run?
The pole bends and stores it, then gives it back and lifts the athlete upward.
Why does height show a strong dependence on speed?
The energy that lifts the athlete comes from the run, so a faster run means more energy.
Why did athletes stop using bamboo?
During the Second World War the supply of good bamboo from Asia was cut off, and metal poles took its place.
What changed after the advent of fiberglass poles?
The poles bent far more and returned the energy smoothly, so records began to rise again.

lessons.title: Eight Blokes and a Boat
lessons.summary: A college rower learns that his crew's speed depends on rhythm, not strength.
lessons.text:
I joined the rowing team in my first year of college, mostly because a tall senior told me I had the right shape for it. I did not know then that the hardest part would be not strength but rhythm.

Our boat was an eight: eight athletes, each pulling one long oar, and a small coxswain who sat at the back, steered and called out the rhythm. On every stroke the blades go into the water together, the legs drive, the backs swing, the arms finish, and then everyone slides forward slowly while the boat runs on beneath us. That slow return is the secret. If one person hurries forward, the boat jerks, like a car when someone hits the brakes, and all eight of us feel it.

Our coach, Ian, was English and had rowed at a university in England. He had a favorite saying: "A crew is eight blokes who trust each other." A bloke, he explained, is what people in England call an ordinary guy, and soon we were calling ourselves the blokes. The best bloke in a boat, Ian said, was not the strongest but the one who could feel the other seven.

We trained on a quiet cove at the north end of a long lake. In the early morning the cove was still and scenic, with mist on the water and pine trees on the hills around it. It was easily the most scenic place I have ever been miserable in.

Because the training was hard, we all became enormous eaters. An athlete in heavy rowing training can burn more than 5,000 calories a day, and our table in the dining hall looked like a wedding feast. Even the lightest eater on the team finished three plates at dinner.

We moaned about everything: the alarm, the cold, the coach. Ian let us moan on land, but never in the boat.

A 2,000-meter race lasts about six minutes, and the last two minutes are pure torment. Your legs burn, your lungs ache, and the discomfort grows so loud that it is hard to hear the coxswain. Ian taught us to expect the discomfort and to row through it. "The torment is the same for both crews," he told us. "The crew that keeps its rhythm wins."

That year the team also got new boats. The university's board of regents had approved an appropriation of $400,000 for equipment. One regent, a libertarian who believed that public money should not pay for sports, voted against the appropriation, and a libertarian student group wrote in the campus paper that he was right. The other regents disagreed, and we were glad.

Then one morning in May, it finally happened. All eight blades entered the water as one, the boat lifted and ran, and for ten minutes it felt as if we were not working at all. Nobody moaned on the way back to the dock.

Questions:
What did Ian mean by "eight blokes who trust each other"?
He meant that a crew is eight ordinary guys who trust each other.
Where did the crew train?
They trained on a quiet cove at the north end of a long lake.
Why did the team become enormous eaters?
An athlete in heavy rowing training can burn more than 5,000 calories a day.
Why did one regent vote against the appropriation?
He was a libertarian who believed that public money should not pay for sports.

lessons.title: Chess on Ice
lessons.summary: A beginner's night at a curling club explains the stones, the sweeping and the strategy.
lessons.text:
When my coworker Dana invited me to a beginners' night at her curling club, I laughed. On television, curling had always looked peculiar to me: one person slides a heavy stone down the ice while two others sweep hard in front of it, and everyone shouts. But Dana is the most sensible coworker I have, so I went.

The instructor, a retired teacher named Joe, promised to simplify the game for us. "Let me simplify it," he said. "You are trying to put your stones closer to the center of the target than the other team's stones. That's it."

The target is called the house, a set of rings painted under the ice at each end of the sheet, which is about 45 meters long. The small circle in the middle, the button, is the focal point of every shot. Each team has four players, and each player throws two stones. After all sixteen stones have been thrown, only the team with the stone closest to the button scores, one point for every stone closer than the other team's best.

The stones are granite, nearly 20 kilograms each, and many come from one small island off the coast of Scotland. The ice is not smooth. Before play, a worker sprays tiny drops of water across it, and they freeze into little bumps. A stone rides on these bumps, and when players sweep in front of it, they warm and polish the ice so that the stone traverses the sheet farther and straighter. The peculiar sweeping, in other words, is serious work.

Joe also showed us why the game is called curling. A player gives the stone a gentle turn on release, and as it slowly traverses the ice, its path bends to one side. Strangely, scientists still argue about exactly why this happens.

Beneath the ice lies a concrete slab full of pipes that carry a very cold liquid, with a thick layer of insulation under it. Without that insulation, the cold would slowly freeze the ground under the building and crack the floor.

Strategy is why curling is often called chess on ice. Teams place guard stones in front of the house to protect their best stones, and Joe said that a guard is like a pawn in chess: cheap, useful and often given up. A good captain, he added, plans several shots ahead.

The game is old. It began on frozen ponds in Scotland centuries ago and was played at the inaugural Winter Olympics in Chamonix, France, in 1924. Joe told us that he now teaches fifth graders on weekend mornings, and that the fifth graders learn faster than adults because they are not afraid to fall.

I did fall, twice. But my last stone stopped inside the house, and Dana cheered. Afterward, when she offered me a hot chocolate, I gladly accepted, and when she asked whether I would come back next week, I gladly said yes.

Questions:
What is the focal point of every shot?
The button, the small circle in the middle of the house, is the focal point.
What does sweeping do?
It warms and polishes the ice, so the stone traverses the sheet farther and straighter.
Why is there insulation under the concrete slab?
Without it, the cold would freeze the ground under the building and crack the floor.
Why does Joe compare a guard stone to a pawn?
Like a pawn in chess, a guard is cheap, useful and often given up.

lessons.title: The Long Road from Marathon
lessons.summary: The legend behind the marathon, the chaotic race of 1904 and the modern event.
lessons.text:
Every marathon begins with a story. In 490 BC, an army from Athens defeated a much larger army sent by the king of Persia on the plain of Marathon, about 40 kilometers from the city. According to the famous version, a messenger ran all the way to the city, announced the victory and fell dead. Today the plain is farmland, and in spring red poppies bloom in its fields. Poppies are a gentle sight for a place with such a violent past.

Herodotus, who wrote about the battle a few decades later, tells a different story. His runner, Pheidippides, ran from Athens to Sparta, about 240 kilometers, to ask for help before the battle. The dramatic run to Athens appears only in writers who lived centuries afterward. True or not, the story inspired a French scholar, Michel Bréal, who suggested a race from Marathon to Athens for 1896, and the marathon was born. Since then, many Games have culminated in a marathon on the final day, and it still feels like the right way for the Games to culminate.

The marathon of 1904, in St. Louis, shows how far the event has come. It was run on a hot August afternoon over dusty country roads, and the cars of officials drove ahead of the runners, raising clouds of dust. There was only one place to get water, a well about 19 kilometers into the race. The chief organizer limited water on purpose because he wanted to study the effects of thirst, an irresponsible experiment by any modern standard.

The race was chaotic. One runner was chased off the course by dogs. Another stopped to eat apples from a tree, felt sick, lay down for a nap and still finished fourth. A third, choking on the dusty air, collapsed by the road with serious injuries. The first man to reach the stadium had ridden much of the way in a car. The real winner was kept going by his team, who gave him small doses of poison mixed with egg and brandy, a remedy as irresponsible as it sounds. Only 14 of the 32 starters finished. In such chaotic conditions, it is astonishing that anyone finished at all.

In London in 1908, the course started at Windsor Castle and finished in front of the royal seats in the stadium, and it came to 42.195 kilometers. In 1921 that strangely precise number became the official length.

The modern marathon is safer and far better organized. Runners start at the gunshot of a starting pistol or the sound of a horn, and in a big city it can take ten minutes or more after the gunshot for the back of the crowd to reach the line. The course follows closed streets, with smooth pavement and water every few kilometers. Many runners stash energy gels in a belt, and some gels contain caffeine, which makes the effort feel a little easier. Hours on hard pavement still hurt, but nobody has to drink from a well.

Questions:
What happened on the plain of Marathon in 490 BC?
An army from Athens defeated a much larger army sent by the king of Persia.
Why was the organizer's decision about water irresponsible?
He limited water on purpose because he wanted to study the effects of thirst.
Why was the 1904 race chaotic?
Runners were chased by dogs, got sick and collapsed, and the first man to arrive had ridden in a car.
What do many modern runners stash in a belt?
They stash energy gels, and some gels contain caffeine.

lessons.title: The Archer Who Breathes
lessons.summary: A profile of an Olympic archer, her grandfather and coach, and her travels.
lessons.text:
On a gray morning at a range outside Portland, Oregon, Sofia Reyes draws her bow, holds it for a few seconds and lets go. Seventy meters away, the arrow lands in the center ring of the target, a circle about as wide as a grapefruit. She simply reaches for the next arrow.

Reyes is 31, works three days a week as a pharmacist and is one of the best archers in the United States. She will compete at her second Olympic Games next summer.

She first held a bow at nine, at a summer camp. It was a simple wooden bow with a walnut grip, and it still hangs on her bedroom wall. The walnut has turned dark from years of sweaty hands. Her competition bow is made of carbon and metal, and it carries a small sight that she adjusts with two tiny knobs: one knob moves the sight up and down for distance, the other moves it left and right for wind. On a windy day she may turn a knob a click or two between arrows.

She builds her own arrows at the kitchen table. She trims small plastic vanes with a pair of scissors and glues three onto each shaft. The scissors were a gift from her grandfather, Frank, who is also her coach.

Frank Reyes is 76, hale and quick to laugh. Five years ago he was treated for prostate cancer, and for a while the family wondered whether he would ever return to the range. He did, within months, and his doctors now call him as hale as a man ten years younger. He talks openly about prostate cancer and tells other men his age to get tested. "Then go shoot some arrows," he adds.

Two years ago she traveled to Istanbul to see the old Field of Arrows, where Ottoman archers once practiced. Stone markers there record famous long shots, and an interpreter helped her read the old writing on them. One marker honors a shot by a sultan in 1798 that is said to have flown nearly 900 meters. The interpreter laughed and told her that on this field, even a sultan was only as good as his last arrow.

In Japan she spent a week with archers who practice kyudo, a traditional art that uses tall bamboo bows. Its archers move slowly and calmly, and for some of them the aim is not only to hit the target but to reach a kind of spiritual enlightenment. Reyes does not claim to have found enlightenment, but she came home knowing how to breathe.

Breathing, she says, is the whole sport. South Korea's women have won every Olympic team title since 1988, and she admires their calm more than their strength. Before each shot, she breathes in, breathes out halfway, and holds. Then she lets go, and the arrow flies.

Questions:
What does Reyes adjust with the two knobs on her sight?
One knob moves the sight up and down for distance, and the other moves it left and right for wind.
What does she do with the small pair of scissors?
She trims the small plastic vanes for her arrows with them.
How is her grandfather doing after his prostate cancer?
He is hale, and his doctors call him as hale as a man ten years younger.
How did the interpreter help her in Istanbul?
The interpreter helped her read the old writing on the stone markers.

lessons.title: From a Hospital Lawn
lessons.summary: A team spokesperson tells how the Paralympic movement began, through her own grandfather's story.
lessons.text:
I work as a spokesperson for a national Paralympic team, and the question I hear most is simple: where did the Paralympics come from? The answer begins on a hospital lawn in England, and, for me, with my own family.

In 1944, a German-born doctor named Ludwig Guttmann, who had fled to Britain a few years earlier, opened a unit for spinal injuries at Stoke Mandeville Hospital, northwest of London. At that time, most people with a spinal cord injury were expected to die within a few years, often from infections and sores. Guttmann changed that. Nurses turned his patients every two hours, careful bladder and bowel care became part of the daily routine, and patients were pushed to sit up, move and work. Bladder and bowel problems had killed many such patients before, and his routine saved lives.

Among those patients was my grandfather, Arthur Bell, a corporal in the army who was badly injured in France in 1944. A destroyer carried him back across the sea to England. He used to say that a sailor on the destroyer gave him a sip of rum from the navy's daily ration, and that it was the worst rum and the kindest gift he had ever received. The corporal who left for France was a runner; the man who came home would never walk again.

Guttmann believed that sport could rebuild both body and confidence. On the day the London Olympic Games opened in 1948, he held an archery contest on the hospital lawn for 16 patients in wheelchairs. My grandfather was one of them. He did not win, but he kept the paper target for the rest of his life.

The contest grew. Dutch veterans joined in 1952, and in 1960 Rome hosted the first Paralympic Games, with about 400 athletes from 23 countries. Since 1988, the Paralympics have been held in the same city as the Olympics, in the same stadiums.

The Games alone did not change how disabled people were treated. Disability activism did much of the work, as people demanded ramps, transport and jobs. Many athletes joined that activism, because they knew that a gold medal meant little if the champion could not get on a bus.

Our fastest runner, who runs on a curved blade of carbon fiber, is nicknamed the Leopard, and when the Leopard races, the crowd is full. Before the London Paralympics of 2012, a TV channel in Britain ran a famous advert, as people in Britain call a commercial, that showed athletes as powerful and fierce rather than as objects of pity. That advert changed the way many viewers saw the Games.

My grandfather lived to watch those Games at the age of 92. As a spokesperson, I tell his story often, and I always end it the same way: it started with 16 people on a lawn.

Questions:
How did Guttmann change the care of patients with spinal injuries?
Nurses turned patients every two hours, careful bladder and bowel care became routine, and patients were pushed to move and work.
How did the corporal get back to England?
A destroyer carried him back across the sea to England.
What happened on the day the London Olympic Games opened in 1948?
Guttmann held an archery contest on the hospital lawn for 16 patients in wheelchairs.
What did the advert show?
It showed athletes as powerful and fierce rather than as objects of pity.

lessons.title: The Curator's Drawer
lessons.summary: A museum curator shows a visitor objects from the 1948 Games, the old art contests and unauthorized souvenirs.
lessons.text:
The small sports museum in our city has one room about the Olympics, and last winter its curator, Ruth Alvarez, gave me a tour. She began at a map of Europe on the wall. In 1915, during the First World War, Coubertin moved the headquarters of the Olympic movement from Paris to Lausanne, in Switzerland. Swiss neutrality, the curator explained, made the country a safe place for an organization that wanted to belong to every nation, and the committee, which still values that neutrality, has stayed there ever since.

Next she showed me a glass case about the London Games of 1948, the first after the Second World War. Britain was still poor, and food was rationed. No new stadiums were built, athletes slept in army camps and colleges, and many brought their own towels. In the case lay a pair of wool socks that a runner had darned at the heels again and again. "She darned them herself the night before her race," the curator said. The Games opened only weeks after the Soviet blockade of Berlin had begun, and the blockade was a reminder that the peace was fragile. Germany and Japan were not invited.

The next case surprised me. From 1912 to 1948, the Games also gave medals for painting, sculpture, music, literature and the design of buildings. In the case lay a flat glass slab and a heavy glass tool with a smooth, flat bottom. The tool is called a muller, the curator told me; painters used a muller to grind colored powder into oil on the slab to make their own paint. A painter who entered the 1948 contest had owned these tools. The art contests ended after that year, partly because most artists were professionals.

Finally, she opened a wide wooden drawer. "This is my favorite," she said. "Unauthorized souvenirs." The five rings are protected, and only official partners may use them commercially. For a century, though, small makers have sold unauthorized copies anyway. In the drawer lay a German beer stein from the Winter Games of 1936, with the rings painted a little crooked on its side, and a toby jug from London, an old English kind of jug shaped like a smiling man in a hat, with the rings on his hat. The stein and the toby jug sat next to a letter opener shaped like a dirk, the long dagger of the Highlands of Scotland, with the rings on its handle. "Nobody would carry a dirk to the Olympics," the curator said, "but someone thought it would sell."

She explained that today companies pay large sums to use the rings commercially, and that this money helps pay for the Games. The objects in her drawer were made without permission, yet she loves them. They show, she said, how much ordinary people wanted to own a small piece of the Olympics.

Questions:
Why did the Olympic headquarters move to Switzerland?
Swiss neutrality made the country a safe place for an organization that wanted to belong to every nation.
What did the runner do to her socks?
She darned them herself at the heels again and again.
What is a muller used for?
Painters used a muller to grind colored powder into oil on a slab to make their own paint.
What lay in the drawer of unauthorized souvenirs?
There was a German beer stein, a toby jug from London and a letter opener shaped like a dirk.
